messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Maya was 19 years old, married, and living in North America with her husband, though she was not working at the time she came for help. Before the assault, she had seen herself as someone who could get through things on her own, and she had built much of her identity around being capable and steady. That understanding of herself changed abruptly after a frightening incident that took place in a setting she had once considered ordinary. One evening, when she was out and it was already dark, she was assaulted by someone who was yelling in Arabic and smelled strongly of alcohol. The details that stayed with her were not broad or vague; they were sensory and immediate, and they returned to her later with the same force. She remembered the sound of shouting in a language she now associated with danger, and the sharp smell of alcohol hanging in the air. Since then, those exact cues have become potent in a way that feels to her almost physical. If she hears Arabic being shouted somewhere nearby, even across a parking lot or through thin apartment walls, her body reacts before she has time to think. If she catches the smell of alcohol on someone passing by, she can feel herself stiffen and go still.

In the weeks after the assault, Maya began to find that reminders could arrive without warning. A sound in the environment, a smell, or an unexpected moment after dark could suddenly bring back the full memory before she had any chance to prepare herself. She described it as if her mind did not ease into the memory but dropped her straight back into it. At times, when she remembered what happened, she would also hear fragments of what she had heard during the event, especially the shouting, as though it were happening again just beside her. On other occasions, when the memory came up, she could smell the alcohol again, and that sensation made the event feel immediate and real rather than distant. There were moments when she would suddenly feel or act as if the assault were happening again, becoming rigid, scanning, and unable to settle until the wave passed. These episodes have been unsettling enough that she has started to worry about being caught off guard anywhere, even in places that should be safe.

Over time, Maya’s days narrowed around what she tried to avoid. She stopped going out at night and became careful about being outside after dark. What had once been a normal part of life now felt exposed and risky to her, especially because the assault itself had happened in the dark and because she found the evening hours more difficult to tolerate. She also began avoiding dates and anniversaries connected to the event, becoming tense as those times approached and trying not to mark them. She could not bear to look closely at her own body or pay attention to it, and she found herself avoiding mirrors and any situation that made her notice herself too much. This was not only about discomfort; it felt to her as though looking would force her to confront something she was not ready to face. She had come to feel that her body itself held too much of what happened.

Maya’s sense of safety in the present has been shaped by constant watching. She listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering the home, especially when she and her husband are at home and the apartment is quiet. She frequently looks behind her to check whether someone is following her, even during brief trips outside during the day. These habits have become part of how she moves through the world, and they have made ordinary outings exhausting. Because she is unemployed, much of her time is spent at home, yet even there she remains on guard, listening for noises at the door or in the hall and trying to keep herself prepared. Her husband has noticed that she is harder to reassure and more reluctant to leave the house after sunset, and this has changed the rhythm of their shared life.

As time has gone on, Maya has become increasingly discouraged by the sense that the assault altered her permanently. She said her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, and she no longer felt that the world was predictable or fair in the way she once assumed. She also believed she was no longer capable of doing the things that defined her. The version of herself that she remembers from before the assault feels, to her, like someone she cannot fully return to. At the same time, she has been stuck with the conviction that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening. That thought leaves her feeling angry and ashamed, as if there should have been a way for the situation to end differently. She came for help now because she is tired of living as if danger is always close, tired of bracing herself every time she hears shouting, catches the smell of alcohol, or has to step outside after dark. What she most hopes for is to feel like herself again, and what she most fears is that the assault has changed the rest of her life in a way she will never be able to undo.
